title: Communicate agri/ecotourism principles and concepts effectively and adapt to needs

lessons.title: Principles of agri-tourism and eco-tourism to communicate
lessons.html:
What you need to explain

Guides, hosts and supervisors on tourism farms must explain what makes the experience special and why visitors should behave in certain ways. Visitors enjoy a farm more when they understand it.

Core principles

  • Authenticity: show real farming and real nature, honestly. Do not stage false stories.
  • Conservation: tourism should help protect soil, water, veld, wildlife and heritage, not damage them.
  • Education and interpretation: help visitors understand what they see, such as why cattle are rotated between camps, how a wine is made, or why a wetland matters.
  • Community benefit: local people should benefit through jobs, local buying and fair treatment.
  • Responsible behaviour: visitors respect the farm, animals, workers and neighbours.
  • Safety: visitors are protected from farm hazards.

Key concepts visitors often ask about

  • Where food comes from and how it is grown or raised
  • Animal welfare on the farm
  • Water use and drought in South Africa
  • Indigenous plants, birds and wildlife
  • Local history, culture and heritage sites
  • Sustainable practices such as composting, solar power and veld management

Interpretation techniques

  • Relate facts to the visitor's own life, for example comparing the water a cow drinks in a day to the visitor's home use.
  • Use stories about the farm and its people.
  • Let visitors touch, smell and taste where safe and permitted.
  • Keep it simple and focused on a few main messages.
  • Ask questions to involve people.

Prepare: know the facts about your farm, its crops, animals and history. If you are unsure, say so and find out rather than guess.

lessons.title: Adapting communication to different visitors
lessons.html:
Know your audience

Visitors differ. Good communicators adjust what they say and how they say it.

Visitor groupAdapt by
School childrenShort, active sessions; hands-on activities; simple words; strict supervision
Foreign touristsClear, slow speech; avoid slang; explain local terms like veld, kraal, braai; check understanding
Farmers and specialistsMore technical detail, data and practices
Elderly visitors or people with disabilitiesAccessible routes, seating, shorter walks, clear audio
FamiliesMix of fun and learning, involve children and adults
Corporate groupsStructured timing, team activities, professional manner

Verbal and non-verbal communication

  • Greet warmly and introduce yourself.
  • Face the group, make eye contact and speak loudly enough for all.
  • Stand so the sun is not in visitors' eyes and noise is behind you.
  • Watch body language: bored, confused or tired faces mean you should change pace.
  • Use visual aids such as maps, samples or photographs where useful.

Language and respect

South Africa has many languages and cultures. Use the language visitors understand best, if you can, or arrange an interpreter. Avoid jokes or remarks that could offend culture, religion, gender or race.

Handling questions and complaints

  • Listen fully, then answer briefly and honestly.
  • If you do not know, say you will find out, and follow up.
  • For complaints: listen, apologise for the experience, act or refer to a manager, and follow up.

Safety briefings

Always start with a short safety briefing adapted to the group: stay on paths, keep away from animals and machinery, what to do if someone is hurt, where the toilets and first aid kit are.

Getting feedback

Ask visitors what they enjoyed and what could be better. Use feedback to improve.

Key points

  • Communicate authenticity, conservation, education, community benefit and safety.
  • Use stories and relate facts to visitors' lives.
  • Adapt language, detail and pace to each group.
  • Always give a safety briefing first.
  • Answer honestly and follow up on complaints and questions.
